Empirical Research Plan – “Do Disappointing Wage Outcomes Reduce Police Performance?”

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DiD) / event–study in a panel of police departments.

Rationale  
• The FOA decision provides a plausibly exogenous, one-time, binary shock to a department’s wage contract.  
• We observe outcomes for the same department before and after the decision, and we have a naturally comparable group (departments that happened to win FOA in the same years).  
• A DiD with department and calendar-year fixed effects nets out (i) time-invariant department differences and (ii) state-wide shocks to crime reporting, policing technology, etc.  
• An event-study extension (relative-year dummies) lets us inspect pre-trends and dynamic treatment effects.

Alternative considered – pure randomized-control framework  
Because FOA decisions are close to random, one could treat “lose FOA” as a randomly assigned treatment and simply compare means post-decision. Nevertheless, adding pre-period outcomes in a DiD greatly improves precision and provides falsification tests (no pre-treatment differences).

------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if a department’s union lost FOA in year t (arbitrator selected management’s wage offer ⇒ salary increase lower than union’s demanded reference point).  
Control = 0 if the union won FOA in year t.

Treatment timing  
Event date = fiscal year of the arbitrator’s decision.  
Post = indicator for each of the three fiscal years following the decision (Post_t = 1 for years 0…+3 relative to decision; 0 for −3…−1).

Sample construction  
• Balanced event-window panel: dept-year observations in the interval [−3, +3].  
• Multiple FOA decisions in a single department are allowed but are spaced several years apart in practice. Each event is coded relative to its own decision; overlapping windows are dropped or the first event kept to avoid contamination.

------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Conditional parallel trends  
Absent the FOA result, departments that lose would have evolved like departments that win.  
Plausibility: Very good. Cases reaching FOA are “close calls,” and the arbitrator’s all-or-nothing choice is unrelated to pre-treatment performance (testable with pre-trend graphs).

A2. No differential anticipation or manipulation  
Officers do not change effort before the decision based on advance knowledge of the outcome; the union can’t manipulate which side wins.  
Plausibility: High. The decision is in the arbitrator’s hands and is often announced well after the wage dispute year.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers)  
One department’s FOA outcome does not affect another’s clearance rate.  
Plausibility: Reasonable—the average municipal PD in NJ has its own command structure; jurisdictional overlap is limited.

A4. Accurate, comparable outcome measurement  
Clearance and arrest data are consistently reported to UCR across departments/years.  
Plausibility: Good but must be checked (missing reports, definitional changes in FBI categories).

------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Selection into FOA (only contentious negotiations reach arbitration).  
Mitigation: Restrict analysis to “arbitration sample,” i.e., departments that had an FOA in this period. This controls for dispute severity. The win/lose split within this sample is quasi-random.

T2. Non-salary contract items may also differ (e.g., staffing levels) and could mechanically affect performance.  
Mitigation: Collect and control for arbitrated decisions on staffing, benefits, or use arbitrator text to build covariates; show effects remain when conditioning on these.

T3. Measurement error in clearance rates or arrests (missing UCR submissions).  
Mitigation: (i) drop department-year observations with <9 months reported, (ii) weight regressions by population served, (iii) replicate results with alternative outcome – crimes occurred per officer (unlikely to be manipulated).

------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -----------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE estimation
library(ggplot2)      # plots
library(readr)

# 1. Load data ----------------------------------------------------
arb <- fread("nj_arbitration_1978_1996.csv")   # dept_id, year, outcome (win=1)
ucr <- fread("ucr_police_1975_1999.csv")       # dept_id, year, crimes, cleared, arrests, population

# 2. Basic merges -------------------------------------------------
dt <- merge(arb, ucr, by=c("dept_id","year"), all.x=TRUE, allow.cartesian=TRUE)

# 3. Variable construction ---------------------------------------
dt[, clearance_rate := cleared / crimes]
dt[, arrests_per_cap := arrests / population]

# Event-time (relative year)
setorder(dt, dept_id, year)
dt[, event_year := year - year[which(outcome %in% c(0,1))[1]], by=dept_id]

# Keep balanced window −3…+3
dt <- dt[event_year >= -3 & event_year <= 3]

# Treatment dummies
dt[, lose := as.integer(outcome == 0)]         # 1 = management win (union lose)
dt[, post := as.integer(event_year >= 0)]

# 4. Main DiD regression -----------------------------------------
spec1 <- feols(clearance_rate ~ lose*post | dept_id + year, 
               data = dt, cluster = ~dept_id)
summary(spec1)

# 5. Event-study (dynamic) ---------------------------------------
for(j in -3:3) dt[, paste0("D",j) := as.integer(event_year==j) * lose] 
dyn_fml <- as.formula(paste("clearance_rate ~",
                    paste(paste0("D", -2:3), collapse="+"), 
                    "| dept_id + year"))
spec2 <- feols(dyn_fml, data=dt[event_year!=-3], cluster=~dept_id)
iplot(spec2)   # built-in event-study graph

# 6. Robustness: arrests outcome ---------------------------------
spec3 <- feols(arrests_per_cap ~ lose*post | dept_id + year, 
               data = dt, cluster = ~dept_id)
summary(spec3)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------------
• Direction: Loss of FOA (smaller raise relative to reference point) → lower effort.  
• Magnitude (back-of-envelope): A 2–3 pp decline in clearance rate (baseline ≈ 30 %) and a 5 % drop in arrests per capita in the three-year window. This is similar to the size of effort responses estimated in lab studies of reference-dependence.

------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = clearly satisfied)
------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Exogenous treatment assignment (lose vs. win) .......... 1  
2. Parallel pre-trends (testable via event-study) ......... 0.8  
3. No spillovers or interference .......................... 0.9  
4. Outcome data quality & consistency .................... 0.7  
5. Sufficient statistical power (383 decisions) .......... 1  
Overall: strong but hinges on validated pre-trends and data quality checks.
